extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, referees, authors, and researchers interested in peer review and editorial policy
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and design of journal peer-review processes and reviewer criteria (e.g., structured guides, blind vs open review, reviewer selection and panel size) to reduce bias and improve quality of editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles should address an important problem (authors should pick important problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Armstrong uses 'importance' as a key positive rating to refute the 'author's formula'—editors/referees should seek evidence that the research addresses questions worth discussing beyond the immediate specialty (e.g., would they discuss it with non-specialists?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge to existing beliefs / novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should challenge existing beliefs rather than merely reiterate them (not avoid challenging current beliefs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should reward attempts to examine or overturn prevailing views; the use of multiple hypotheses to test alternatives is noted as a strong method. This dimension combats tendencies to favor conservative, confirmatory work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising results / substantive contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should obtain and present results that are surprising or non-obvious (not avoid surprising results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprising findings are evidence of substantive contribution; reviewers should recognize and value unexpected but well-supported results rather than dismiss them as implausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and transparency of methods (including simple methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of simple, appropriate methods should not be penalized (not avoid simple methods); methodological simplicity can be acceptable if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Armstrong argues that simple methods can be valuable; reviewers should evaluate whether methods appropriately address the question rather than preferring complexity for its own sake. Beware of using 'methodological flaws' as a generic pretext to dismiss work without specific evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure and access to original data
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should provide full disclosure and access to original data so findings can be verified (not fail to provide full disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of disclosure undermines confidence and opens the door to hoaxes or analytic errors; editors/reviewers should request data, list of referees (when relevant), and other materials needed to evaluate the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and readability of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should be written clearly and accessibly (not write obtusely); clarity should be positively rated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures like the Gunning fog index are cited to illustrate readability; obtuse writing can hide flaws and may perversely confer perceived prestige, but clarity should be rewarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of structured guides for referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should employ structured review guides that clarify aims and reduce bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Armstrong suggests structured guides be designed to 'refute the author's formula' by explicitly asking referees to rate importance, novelty, surprisingness, methodological appropriateness (including simple methods), disclosure, and clarity. Structured guides help align reviewers and reduce influence of irrelevant factors (e.g., author prestige).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review / publication of reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider open peer review where referees' identities or reports are disclosed/published alongside papers to increase accountability and communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open review may be resisted by some referees, but Armstrong and others note benefits: greater equity, efficiency, motivation for careful reviewing, opportunities for discussion between authors and referees, and recognition for referees' work. Formats include publishing referee reports with articles (as done by Behavioral and Brain Sciences' commentary model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind refereeing to reduce bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of blind (anonymous) refereeing is recommended to reduce bias related to author identity or institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies show blind reviewing is not harmful and can be helpful; costs are negligible. Armstrong cites evidence that reviewers seldom detect previously published work or correctly guess authorship for most papers, so blind review is expected to be relevant for most submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel size and multiple reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple reviewers (more than the conventional one-to-three) to reduce chance and individual bias—CA uses ~15, BBS uses 5–8 precontacted referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger reviewer samples help reveal differences of opinion and counteract bias, but too large a panel can increase noise, hamper revisionability, and resemble committee writing. A balance is needed; Armstrong/Belshaw discuss thresholds (e.g., CA often requires ~80% approval) and practical trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection criteria and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Select reviewers based on expertise, past record (e.g., responsiveness, avoidance of ad hominem), international and disciplinary diversity, and avoid overusing the same reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belshaw describes selecting reviewers internationally (to reflect the field), including interdisciplinary experts when necessary, and using factors like prior reliability. Use of computer-assisted selection to identify qualified specialists is recommended when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precontacting referees to ensure willingness and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Precontact referees (e.g., by phone) to confirm willingness and ability to meet deadlines to improve return rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBS precontacts referees which yields near-100% response and higher effective return rates compared to unsolicited requests; this reduces late or missing reviews and improves editorial scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage substantive, specific reviewer reports (not generic criticisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should expand on checklist responses with specific, cogent criticisms rather than relying on vague methodological-flaw accusations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific reasons are crucial for editors when assessing disagreement or bias and invaluable for authors revising papers. Generic critiques can be used as a way to dismiss papers without exposing the basis for rejection; editors should seek specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial moderation of ad hominem or destructive commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should moderate/remove excessively scathing, ad hominem, or potentially libelous comments, balancing debate with protection of authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belshaw notes the necessity to censor extremely destructive comments; linking refereeing to public commentary increases accountability but also raises editorial burdens to manage tone and avoid harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance decision rules / threshold and weight of cogent criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial policies should state decision thresholds (e.g., a high percentage approval like 80%) while allowing a single cogent, substantive criticism to outweigh many bland approvals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belshaw describes that even if most reviewers approve, one serious flaw in methodology, data, or fundamentals can justify rejection; journals should be explicit about how conflicting reviews are weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for evidence when claiming redundancy / prior publication
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewers assert a paper merely repeats previously published work, they should provide evidence; mere intuition is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beaver/others stress that claiming work is 'old' must be supported, otherwise authors can rebut. Reviewers sometimes prefer to cite vague 'methodological flaws' to avoid rebuttal; editorial policy should require specific evidence for redundancy claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commentary/public post-acceptance review to catch issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide mechanisms (commentary panels or published comments) post-acceptance to catch problems like duplicate publication or encourage wider debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBS/CA invite commentators (often many) after acceptance; multiple commentators and continuing commentary sections can reveal problems not caught in initial review and broaden input, but may also surface ad hominem disputes requiring editorial control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and monitor reviewer detection/knowledge limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and empirically assess that reviewers read only a small fraction of the literature and often fail to detect prior publication; design policies accordingly (e.g., blind review, larger panels, better selection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical citations show low readership per article and low detection rates of prior publication. Editors should not assume reviewers will catch redundancy or plagiarism without explicit checks and should consider structural remedies.
